name: deku
vendor: Open-source project started by Emmanuel Thompson (sharksforarms)
summary: A Rust derive macro that turns an annotated struct or enum into a bit-level reader and writer for the same binary layout.
intro: You add `#[derive(DekuRead, DekuWrite)]` to a struct or enum and describe the layout with `#[deku(...)]` attributes: `endian = "big"`, `bits = 4` for a field narrower than a byte, `magic = b"SN"` for fixed leading bytes, `count = "count"` for an array whose length was read earlier, and `id` or `id_type` to pick an enum variant from a tag in the input. `ctx` passes values such as byte order or an earlier field down to nested types. The derive generates `from_bytes` and `from_reader` for reading, from a byte slice or any `io::Read + Seek` source, and `to_bytes` and `to_writer` for writing. Byte-aligned fields are read with the standard library; when a layout needs bit-level control, deku uses the `bitvec` crate underneath.

Because one definition drives both directions, a value read and written back comes out byte for byte, and Rust still chooses how the struct sits in memory; only the wire form is packed. deku runs without the standard library when its `alloc` feature is on, and fixed-size types get a `DekuSize` trait whose `SIZE_BYTES` constant sizes a static buffer at compile time, which suits embedded code. It is still at version 0.x: 0.20 shipped in October 2025, and several recent releases changed the API.
strengths: Fields of any bit width anywhere in a struct, most significant bit first by default and least significant first since 0.19
One derive gives a reader and a writer that agree with each other, including tagged enums with a `default` variant for unknown ids
Works in `no_std` builds with only `alloc`, and `DekuSize` gives compile-time sizes for fixed-size messages
A `logging` feature reports each step of a read at trace level, which helps find where a parse went wrong
limits: Counts don’t follow the data: push to a `Vec` and its `count` field stays stale until you call `update()`
Still 0.x with breaking releases: 0.17 (2024) moved reading to `io::Read` and renamed `type` to `id_type`, and 0.18 made readers require `Seek`
Bit-level support costs speed when you don’t need it; the docs suggest turning off the default `bits` feature for byte-only formats
A parent’s byte order must be passed to child types through `ctx`, and forgetting it shows up as a “mismatched types” error from the derive

sections.title: deku, binrw or Construct?
sections.intro: All three derive a reader and a writer from one description of the layout. They differ in language, in how small a field can be, and in how they keep a count in step with its array.

rows.label: Smallest field
values: One byte; bit fields through crates such as `bilge`

story: Without a tool like this, a Rust program that speaks a binary protocol needs two hand-written functions per message: one that reads the bytes and one that writes them back, kept in step by hand. Emmanuel Thompson, who publishes as sharksforarms, started deku to remove that “redundant, error-prone” pair. The first release reached crates.io in March 2020, and eight more minor versions followed before the end of that year.

The crate was built on `bitvec`, so fields could be any number of bits from the start. As it found users, much of the work moved to performance: in 2022 a byte-only fast path for reading, and in 2024 version 0.17 replaced slice-based reading with streaming from `io::Read`, which its changelog credits with “massive performance and usability improvements”. Contributor wcampbell0x2a, who wrote that byte fast path, is now a co-owner of the crate. The same year bit-level support became an optional feature, and 0.19 in 2025 added least-significant-bit-first ordering for formats that need it.

choices.why: The README’s pitch is symmetry: the reader and writer come from the same attributes, so they can’t disagree about the layout.

choices.choice: Let Rust choose the memory layout
choices.why: The struct isn’t `#[repr(C, packed)]` or transmuted from bytes; deku reads and writes the packed wire form while the compiler lays out the struct as it likes.
Network headers and TLVs pack flags and small numbers into partial bytes, so `bits = N` works on any field, at the cost of a `bitvec` dependency that later became optional.
Reading from any source, including a file, without loading it whole made 0.17 faster, at the cost of removing attributes that looked at the rest of the input.

timeline.text: First release on crates.io (March); 0.9 by October
Fixes undefined behaviour in its slice code and yanks affected versions; a faster byte-only read path
0.17 reads from `io::Read`; 0.18 adds seek attributes and makes bit support optional
0.19 adds `bit_order = "lsb"`; 0.20 adds an `alloc` feature for heapless targets
